Same-toolkit overlap with SourceDefense not resolved; no VexTrio attribution. Merchants are victims, never blocklist labels. Split encrypted-envelope parser branch not seen used.

Exact full RPC pool not printed in article/IOC text. Two injected loader URLs are compromised websites, not dedicated malicious domains.

techniques.title: Smart-contract payload hosting
techniques.summary: Encoded loader code lives in contract state and is retrieved by a browser or downloader.
techniques.mechanism: Public reports describe JavaScript stored in BNB Smart Chain and Base contract state and retrieved by browser loaders. Mainnet and testnet examples are documented. A getter that returns only an off-chain URL is address resolution (LBC-003), not payload hosting.
techniques.detection: Correlate unexpected RPC reads with script execution, redirects and browser child processes. eth_call reads are visible to the RPC provider, not recorded as transactions.
techniques.mitigation: Restrict unsanctioned RPC egress, review web scripts and browser service workers, and block confirmed downstream delivery resources.

techniques.title: Transaction calldata as a payload store
techniques.summary: Malware retrieves encoded payloads from transaction input data rather than a file server.
techniques.mechanism: GTIG describes BSC contract staging followed by Ethereum transaction-history reads, including transactions to a burn address. Explorer APIs return the payload data. Chainalysis also covers BSC input-data stages reached through TRON/Aptos.
techniques.detection: Hunt unusual transaction-history API access followed by in-memory execution. Capture transaction hashes as well as domains.
techniques.mitigation: Use API-aware egress monitoring. A burn address is not a network endpoint; block the retrieval path or identified payload infrastructure.

techniques.title: Contract-based C2 address resolution
techniques.examples: EtherRAT; Tsundere; RedLine-lineage resolver; REVSTEALER; AnimateClipper / Zig; HexMage
techniques.summary: A stable contract supplies the current off-chain C2 location.
techniques.mechanism: Contract getters supply an off-chain destination. Sysdig documents nine-provider majority voting; Hunt.io lists seven configured providers and periodic refresh; RedLine-lineage samples decrypt BSC resolver data. REVSTEALER uses an encrypted Polygon fallback. PasteSwitch mirrors BSC testnet/mainnet updates and disguises a getter as balanceOf. HexMage uses Sepolia pointers. A provider, contract, downstream C2 and exfiltration server are distinct objects. Chainalysis separately identifies Polygon resolvers and BSC resolver fleets administered by shared operators.
techniques.detection: Correlate RPC fan-out or repeated getters with newly contacted destinations. Retain chain ID, selector, address, process and request timing. Familiar ERC-20 selectors such as balanceOf do not prove a benign token lookup.
techniques.mitigation: Baseline RPC use by host and process. Deny unsanctioned providers and investigate the returned destination.

techniques.title: On-chain command and configuration retrieval
techniques.summary: Contract state carries instructions that infected devices retrieve and interpret.
techniques.mechanism: Aeternum retrieves encrypted commands through Polygon RPC. REVSTEALER modules retrieve replaceable settings; one getter supplies mining command-line arguments. These are instruction/configuration reads, distinct from a getter that returns only a C2 URL. Published code configuration does not prove every branch ran.
techniques.detection: Correlate repeating eth_call traffic, contract addresses and execution of downloaded components.
techniques.mitigation: Control RPC egress and investigate loader persistence. Provider blocking alone will not remove the contract.

techniques.title: Bitcoin OP_RETURN dead drops
techniques.examples: Glupteba; suspected Iran-nexus operator reported by Chainalysis
techniques.summary: Encrypted backup C2 domains are embedded in Bitcoin transactions.
techniques.mechanism: Glupteba recovers backup C2 domains from encrypted Bitcoin OP_RETURN data. Google documents disruption; earlier Trend Micro analysis describes Electrum queries for transaction history. Explorer APIs and Electrum servers are different retrieval paths. Chainalysis reports a suspected Iran-nexus OP_RETURN resolver using a public reference address; that reference is not attacker-owned.
techniques.detection: Look for transaction lookups from unexpected processes followed by new HTTPS destinations, especially after C2 failures. Differentiate the transaction sender, reference recipient and OP_RETURN contents; a public reference recipient is not an attribution verdict.
techniques.mitigation: Monitor explorer APIs and Bitcoin clients; hunt wallet strings in samples. Revalidate historical domains before blocking.

attack.rationale: OP_RETURN contains a pointer to an off-chain C2 domain, used when primary servers fail. This supports both dead-drop resolution and a fallback channel.

techniques.title: C2 encoded in transaction amounts
techniques.summary: Transaction values act as an encoded configuration channel.
techniques.mechanism: Published investigations describe converting Bitcoin transaction amounts into a backup C2 IP. RTM also used alternative naming. Historical APIs and current RPC services should not be assumed interchangeable.
techniques.detection: Correlate explorer requests with outbound connections to newly seen IPs. URL reputation alone does not reveal the encoded destination.
techniques.mitigation: Baseline explorer traffic from servers and shell processes; block validated downstream infrastructure.

attack.rationale: Explorer-accessed transaction values recover a backup C2 IP. This is a pointer and fallback mechanism; it is not DNS tunneling.

techniques.title: Recipient-address C2 signaling
techniques.summary: A transaction recipient field encodes the current C2 location.
techniques.mechanism: Recipient bytes encode a downstream address. HashHiding scans Ethereum blocks alongside the RAT’s parallel recovery routes; NullReceiver selects an outbound zero-value transfer and decodes its recipient. Neither requires a smart-contract payload. Transaction totals are signaling activity, not infection counts.
techniques.detection: Hunt eth_getBlockByNumber and eth_blockNumber from unexpected Node.js processes, followed by direct-IP HTTP traffic.
techniques.mitigation: Monitor both chain reads and resulting C2 connections; cover fallback channels during containment.

techniques.title: Cross-chain payload routing
techniques.examples: UNC5342-linked redundant TRON / Aptos routes, per Chainalysis
techniques.summary: Different chains provide redundant pointers to a payload stored on another chain.
techniques.mechanism: The loader tries a TRON transaction route, then Aptos on failure. Both point to BSC transaction input holding encrypted instructions or configuration. Decryption leads to off-chain infrastructure. Chainalysis associates the deployer with UNC5342; this is its attribution assessment.
techniques.detection: Correlate ordered TRON-to-Aptos fallback with BSC transaction lookups, then downstream connections. Preserve transaction identifiers and decoded pointer relationships; normal traffic on any one chain is insufficient.
techniques.mitigation: Contain the loader and validated downstream services. Review alternate RPC routes and self-hosted nodes; provider lists alone cannot guarantee disruption across every route.
techniques.chain_evidence_note: The reviewed text and case-study figures describe routes without complete account addresses or transaction hashes. No explorer target is reconstructed.

attack.rationale: The chain queries resolve staging/C2 infrastructure, with Aptos providing a fallback to the TRON route. Mapping is limited to the pointer and fallback behavior.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: On-chain victim tracking
techniques.summary: Victim identifiers and IP addresses are recorded in a public transaction ledger.
techniques.mechanism: INDA documents BSC-testnet victim IP telemetry. Expel separately analyzes a contract used to check visitor UUIDs during delivery. Distinguish a duplicate-visitor flag from an IP-bearing public record, and do not interpret raw ledger counts as unique infected devices. Talos reconstructs cjs_id visitor checks during ClearFake delivery; a cookie UUID check alone does not establish stolen-file or IP exfiltration.
techniques.detection: Hunt unexpected testnet writes and preserve transaction input data as potentially sensitive incident evidence.
techniques.mitigation: Restrict unsanctioned testnet access; remove the loader. Public victim records may persist after remediation.

techniques.title: Blockchain DNS for C2 and delivery
techniques.examples: RTM; Dofoil / Smoke Loader; Terdot; GandCrab
techniques.summary: Blockchain-backed names provide an alternative to conventional DNS registration.
techniques.mechanism: Microsoft and Mandiant document .bit resolution in malware, including use of alternative resolvers to find C2 or download infrastructure.
techniques.detection: Inspect .bit lookups, custom Namecoin API reads and DNS sent to external resolvers. Correlate name-operation changes with resolved connections. A wallet funding a name is context, not an automatic maliciousness verdict.
techniques.mitigation: Enforce approved DNS paths and inspect resolved connections. Treat historical .bit indicators as investigation leads.

attack.rationale: Blockchain names support C2 discovery, but the entry does not establish DGA, fast flux, DNS calculations or commands tunneled in DNS. No specific technique is forced from the .bit suffix.

techniques.title: Emercoin naming for malicious infrastructure
techniques.summary: Alternative blockchain namespaces support resilient infrastructure naming.
techniques.mechanism: Mandiant documents malicious use of Emercoin namespaces such as .bazar and .coin, including gateway-based access.
techniques.detection: Monitor alternative namespaces and unapproved resolver or gateway use. A matching suffix alone is not proof of malware.
techniques.mitigation: Apply DNS and egress policy using organizational need; investigate the resolved destination and process.

attack.rationale: Alternative names support access to malicious infrastructure. A .bazar or .coin name by itself does not demonstrate a particular dynamic-resolution or DNS-tunneling technique.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Content-addressed payload and phishing hosting
techniques.examples: Dark Utilities; TransferLoader; DEAD#VAX; AsyncAPI; IPFS phishing
techniques.summary: HTTP gateways expose content addressed by CID across multiple providers.
techniques.mechanism: IPFS HTTP gateways expose CID-addressed files and phishing pages. Reports show binaries, scripts and a VHD. The same CID can be served through different path or subdomain gateways. Phishing credentials and subsequent malware traffic commonly leave through conventional endpoints; hosting does not establish IPFS exfiltration.
techniques.detection: Extract and normalize CIDs from /ipfs/ paths and subdomain gateways; correlate downloads with execution.
techniques.mitigation: Block validated CIDs or resources across gateways; baseline shared gateway use and self-hosted peers.

attack.rationale: These mappings apply to the malware-hosting and tool-retrieval portion of this entry. A phishing HTML page or ordinary CID request alone does not establish either behavior.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Peer-to-peer C2 over IPFS infrastructure
techniques.summary: Malware uses a peer-to-peer communication layer built on IPFS infrastructure.
techniques.mechanism: Intezer documents cross-platform IPStorm variants using IPFS to conceal botnet communications. This extends beyond public HTTP gateways.
techniques.detection: Look for unexpected peer networking, new long-lived sessions and unknown executables. Gateway-only detections are incomplete.
techniques.mitigation: Use endpoint visibility and egress application controls; identify unauthorized peer clients and persistence.

attack.rationale: IPStorm uses a peer overlay for C2. The catalog does not establish a precise ATT&CK transport technique; peer-to-peer routing alone is not automatically Non-Application Layer Protocol.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Generated content identifiers for C2 discovery
techniques.summary: Generated resource identifiers replace a fixed list of domains or content pointers.
techniques.mechanism: The Hydras paper experimentally studies IPFS-based bot management and identifier generation. This entry is a research demonstration, not an attributed campaign.
techniques.detection: Consider repeated content retrieval attempts and unknown IPFS clients; validate against legitimate distributed applications.
techniques.mitigation: Retain CID and peer telemetry; apply policy to unsanctioned distributed-storage clients.

attack.rationale: Research-context association for generated resource identifiers used in bot management. Content-identifier generation is not automatically a domain-generation algorithm.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: NKN overlay command and control
techniques.summary: Blockchain-oriented peer routing transports commands between malware and operators.
techniques.mechanism: Malware uses NKN seed discovery and peer messaging for control. AhnLab publishes NKNShell seed traffic and the returned relay. NKNShell also supports MQTT, which is a separate non-blockchain channel. A relay carrying a session is not thereby attacker-owned.
techniques.detection: Hunt unexpected NKN client processes and seed access, then correlate subsequent peer connections.
techniques.mitigation: Restrict unauthorized NKN use by application and egress policy. Do not classify relay peers as attacker-owned merely from transit.

attack.rationale: NKN relays commands through a shared peer overlay. This supports the C2 tactic, but does not by itself justify a Web Service or Non-Application Layer Protocol technique.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Data return over NKN messaging
techniques.summary: The same overlay carries host information and command results out of the victim network.
techniques.mechanism: NKAbuse returns screenshots, heartbeat and command output over NKN. AhnLab also documents NKNShell sending system information through NKN and an independent MQTT path. Overlay messages do not imply public ledger storage.
techniques.detection: Correlate screen capture or collection behavior with NKN-enabled processes and outbound peer traffic.
techniques.mitigation: Contain the endpoint and its NKN client; shared relay blocking should be driven by business policy.

attack.rationale: NKAbuse returns screenshots, host information and command results over its existing NKN C2 channel. Data is not necessarily written to a blockchain ledger.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: TON overlay transport for remote control
techniques.summary: An embedded proxy carries malicious traffic through TON’s encrypted overlay.
techniques.mechanism: ThreatFabric documents .adnl destinations routed through a local TON proxy, alongside remote-control and file-upload capabilities. The pseudo-hostnames are not ordinary DNS records.
techniques.detection: Inspect Android app provenance, native proxy components and unexpected TON flows. DNS-only blocklists cannot cover ADNL identities.
techniques.mitigation: Use mobile endpoint controls and application-aware egress policy. There is no complete static list of TON peer IPs here.

attack.rationale: Mobile-matrix tactic associations for Android remote control and information return. TON overlay transport alone is insufficient for a precise Mobile technique, and Enterprise IDs are not substituted.

techniques.title: ICP canister as a dead-drop resolver
techniques.summary: A canister-hosted HTTP resource returns the next payload location.
techniques.mechanism: Aikido documents a Python backdoor polling a specific ICP canister for a download URL. The full canister hostname is a more precise control than the shared parent domain.
techniques.detection: Hunt periodic requests to canister hosts from interpreters and developer or CI endpoints.
techniques.mitigation: Block confirmed canister resources, investigate compromised packages, and rotate affected developer credentials.

attack.rationale: The canister supplies a separate payload URL; the implant then downloads the payload. MITRE also lists CanisterWorm under Dead Drop Resolver, but this catalog mapping remains an analyst assessment.

techniques.title: Ransomware communication proxy discovery

techniques.detection: Investigate ransom-note HTML traffic and Polygon lookups in affected hosts. Preserve returned proxy URLs.
techniques.mitigation: Block validated proxy resources and contain the intrusion. Shared RPC blocks can affect legitimate applications.

techniques.title: Split-secret encrypted contract configuration
techniques.summary: Recovering a destination requires both on-chain ciphertext and site-held secret material.
techniques.mechanism: Source Defense reports contract values carrying encrypted configuration while a compromised website supplies separate password material. The public chain object alone does not disclose the destination. This is storage encryption, not evidence that every C2 transport is encrypted. Confiant independently identifies encrypted variants and their loader-held secrets. Only individually evidenced encrypted destinations are linked to this record; the wider tracker includes plaintext cases.
techniques.detection: Preserve the injected web loader with the contract response. Link decryption activity to the resolved destination; a contract-only extraction may be incomplete.
techniques.mitigation: Remove site injection and investigate the resulting destination. Keep secrets from incident evidence private; use contract and source context for network controls.

techniques.title: TON smart-contract C2 resolution
techniques.summary: A TON getter supplies a changing domain for an off-chain WebSocket session.
techniques.mechanism: ITOCHU documents a TON API get_domain request and a changed value in June 2026. The account is redacted in the publication. This uses contract resolution, distinct from TrickMo TON overlay transport.
techniques.detection: Look for unexpected TON API getter requests followed by new WebSocket connections. Preserve route, method and returned domain where available.
techniques.mitigation: Baseline TON API use; block validated downstream resources and remove the implant. Do not infer a full contract address from the redacted source.
techniques.chain_evidence_note: The published TonRAT account is redacted. No complete contract address or explorer link is reconstructed.

attack.rationale: The published TON getter returns a separate WebSocket C2 location. This is address resolution, distinct from a TON overlay C2 transport.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Blockchain-controlled server-side loader mesh
techniques.summary: A persistent web-server loader mesh recovers control infrastructure through blockchain reads.
techniques.mechanism: Sucuri describes cooperating WordPress persistence locations. The payload uses public Ethereum RPC gateways and smart-contract selectors as a control channel; response details and the network ID are not published. It encrypts site information and administrator-session material and POSTs it to an off-chain resolved endpoint. The report publishes no complete contract address or exact gateway hosts.
techniques.detection: Review PHP egress, WordPress drop-ins, plugins, database persistence and unexpected administrator-session access. Join RPC reads to subsequent outbound POSTs.
techniques.mitigation: Remove all cooperating persistence locations and rotate exposed sessions and secrets. Rebuilding only one plugin may leave the mesh intact.
techniques.chain_evidence_note: The cited investigation does not publish a complete contract address. No contract link is inferred from the RPC provider.

attack.rationale: Ethereum resolution supplies the off-chain control location. Persistence and exfiltration are contextual tactic associations for the server-side mesh and outbound site/session data; no single persistence sub-technique is forced across all placements.

wild_ranking.basis: Cited research breadth; not measured prevalence

techniques.title: Blockchain fallback in multi-channel bootstrapping
techniques.summary: An implant bundles chain and distributed-storage recovery alongside conventional channels.
techniques.mechanism: AsyncAPI reports establish IPFS staging and Ethereum configuration in a multi-channel loader. A configured Ethereum route is not proof of an observed command exchange. Microsoft states that credential harvesting, encrypted exfiltration and propagation modules were disabled in the analyzed build.
techniques.detection: Separate active IPFS requests from fallback configuration discovered in files. Correlate CI/package import activity with interpreter egress.
techniques.mitigation: Remove affected releases and investigate execution. Cover fallback surfaces using approved application policy without treating disabled modules as observed exfiltration.

techniques.title: Blockchain-staged browser WebRTC payload channel
techniques.summary: An on-chain browser loader receives its next code stage through a WebRTC data channel.
techniques.mechanism: BSC-testnet eth_call returns JavaScript with a hardcoded SDP answer and ICE/DTLS parameters. This avoids a separate external signaling exchange, then opens a UDP WebRTC data channel and buffers attacker code. DOM injection reuses a page CSP nonce, with a Function fallback. The payload channel is off-chain; no on-chain exfiltration is established.
techniques.detection: Join browser contract reads to unexpected UDP/WebRTC destinations and subsequent script execution. HTTP-only gateway logs may miss the data channel; preserve browser and endpoint telemetry.
techniques.mitigation: Remove injected web loaders and investigate downloaded stages. Review WebRTC egress policy and confirmed remote resources; RPC blocking alone does not cover an already loaded UDP stage.

attack.reference: MITRE ATT&CK live pages reviewed on the stated date; no release version is inferred.
attack.policy: Behavior-based analyst associations, not MITRE endorsement or proof of campaign coverage. Research and implemented capabilities retain their original evidence status. Tactic-only and unmapped entries are deliberate.

wild_ranking.label: Top 10 in the wild
wild_ranking.meaning: The ten Observed techniques with the broadest cited threat-research coverage in this library. A source-coverage proxy, not a measured global top ten.
wild_ranking.inclusion: Only Observed techniques with directly supporting Threat research sources qualify. Explicitly labeled related-context references do not vote for that technique. All source-library entries are considered by type; official documentation, ATT&CK definitions and research demonstrations do not contribute votes.
wild_ranking.limitations: The library is curated and publication-biased. Multiple reports can describe the same campaign; these are not counted as separate infections or unique campaigns. One campaign can support several technique patterns. Endpoint, wallet, contract and victim counts are not ranking inputs. No recency window or global usage rate is inferred.
wild_ranking.refresh: Recomputed by build_data.py after source and technique references are reviewed and updated. New publications can change membership. Updating documentation alone cannot improve a technique score.

rpc_directory.scope: Legitimate community RPC directory, separate from report-linked infrastructure. Host/origin only; paths, query strings, fragments, userinfo, template URLs and nonpublic hosts are excluded. Not a working RPC client list or a denylist.
